sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities rebounded as robust Big Tech earnings and a semiconductor recovery outweighed a fresh round of US tariffs and a sharp back-up in bond yields. MSCI World rose roughly **1%**, MSCI Developed Markets was similar, and MSCI Emerging Markets edged higher, around **+0.5%**. The S&P 500 gained about **1%** to **7,489.72** and the Nasdaq Composite climbed roughly **1.6%** to **25,373.85**, though the MAG7 cohort was highly dispersed: Microsoft and Amazon jumped near **9%** while Alphabet slid about **15%** and Meta some **9.6%**. In Europe the STOXX 600 added **0.46%** and the Euro Stoxx 50 gained about **1.5%**; China's CSI 300 rose roughly **0.9%** to **4,588**, Hong Kong's Hang Seng was little changed near **25,859**, and Japan's Nikkei 225 rebounded sharply to about **64,362**.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities recovered, snapping the prior week's semiconductor rout as chips roared back. The S&P 500 rose about **1%** to **7,489.72**, the Nasdaq Composite advanced roughly **1.6%** to **25,373.85** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added around **1%** to **52,485.03**, with information technology and communication services leading the bounce even as the Nasdaq still closed July down **3.2%**.

Earnings dominated a light data week, with 86 S&P 500 constituents and five of the MAG7 reporting. Microsoft and Amazon surged near **9%** on revenue and margin beats, while Apple slipped **3%** to **4%** despite a top-line beat; Alphabet tumbled roughly **15%** and Meta about **9.6%** as heavy AI capital-expenditure plans unnerved investors, leaving reactions hinging on how convincingly each firm defended its AI spend.

The Fed held its target range at **3.5%-3.75%** with three dissents favouring a hike, and Chair Warsh struck a hawkish tone. Sentiment was further tested by a fresh round of Trump-administration tariffs on dozens of partners and by WTI crude near **$84**, which pushed Treasury yields sharply higher and pressured rate-sensitive names.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities advanced and closed out a positive month, with the pan-European STOXX Europe 600 rising **0.46%** in local-currency terms to fresh record territory as technology shares and upbeat earnings underpinned sentiment.

Regional bourses were broadly firmer: the UK's FTSE 100 climbed **1.28%**, Germany's DAX added **1.08%**, France's CAC 40 rose **0.40%** and the Euro Stoxx 50 gained roughly **1.5%**. Resilient corporate results and the global chip recovery supported cyclicals, though gains were uneven beneath the index level.

The main headwind was Washington's announcement of new tariffs on dozens of trading partners, including the EU and the UK, which capped risk appetite late in the week. Hawkish signals from the ECB's July meeting and elevated oil kept the rates and inflation backdrop firmly in focus.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets rebounded, led by a powerful recovery in Japan. The Nikkei 225 surged around **4%** to about **64,362** as heavyweight chip and AI-linked shares bounced back, and the Bank of Japan left policy unchanged after a volatile run-up.

The yen dominated the macro narrative: Japanese authorities intervened to defend the currency ahead of the BoJ decision, and the yen spiked as much as **3.3%** against the dollar intraday, tightening financial conditions and complicating the export-heavy equity backdrop even as shares rallied.

Chinese equities were steadier, with the mainland CSI 300 rising roughly **0.9%** to **4,588** and Hong Kong's Hang Seng little changed near **25,859**. A regional semiconductor recovery and resilient tech-sector momentum supported sentiment, though the fresh US tariff round kept trade-policy risk elevated across Asia ex-Japan.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar softened late in the week, retreating after the Fed left policy unchanged and as a yen shock reset positioning across the G10, leaving the greenback mixed overall as rate differentials again drove price action.

The yen was the standout: Tokyo intervened to defend the currency ahead of the BoJ, and USD/JPY was the worst-performing G10 pair, with the yen jumping as much as **3.3%** intraday and firming close to **2%** on the week, keeping intervention risk front of mind.

The euro pushed to one-month highs, though EUR/USD edged marginally lower on the week despite hawkish ECB signals as the dollar retained an edge. Sterling underperformed, heading for its weakest week in five against the dollar and its poorest against the euro since May after the Bank of England held rates.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Energy remained the dominant cross-asset driver. Brent crude traded above **$89** and WTI near **$84**, on pace for their largest monthly advance since March, as the ongoing US-Iran conflict continued to strain supply through the Strait of Hormuz and backwardation flattered returns.

Precious metals steadied after recent weakness, with gold rangebound near **$4,100** an ounce and on course for its first monthly gain since February, as firmer real yields and a choppy dollar left bullion searching for direction.

The higher-oil, sticky-inflation mix tightened financial conditions and fed directly into the week's sharp rise in bond yields and a softer tone in high-yield credit, sharpening the divergence between a resilient energy complex and more rate-sensitive assets.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign yields rose sharply following the Fed meeting, with the steepest moves at the long end steepening the curve. The 10-year UST reached **4.737%** intraday, its highest since January 2025, while the 30-year hovered near **5.22%**, a level not seen since 2007, as rising oil and tariff-driven inflation risks weighed on duration.

The Fed held its target range at **3.5%-3.75%**, with three policymakers dissenting in favour of a quarter-point hike. Chair Warsh reiterated the commitment to restoring price stability and signalled readiness to act if needed, keeping the bar for near-term easing high.

Credit tone deteriorated modestly, with high-yield bonds generating negative returns amid a more risk-off backdrop driven by higher oil, sticky inflation, rate-hike fears, AI-growth uncertainty and Middle East tension. Investment-grade proved more resilient, but the setup argued for continued selectivity and a bias towards quality.
